chapter.p: Whenever any non-trivial and narratively interesting action happens within the game the players should be involved in a Check to determine the outcome. Checks are the mechanic we use to for all conflict in the Malleus Deum.

For example, a PC might make a check to climb a wall, to stab an enemy, close a protective circle, block an attack, cast a spell, resist their fear of heights, or jump a horse over a fence. Similarly NPCs and monsters can make checks to attack PCs. In fact, Checks can me made by any antagonist, the environment might make a hyperthermia check against the PCs, and the PCs would have to react to save against that effect.

section.p: Checks are based on the concept of Actor-Check-Reactor triplets, in which an Actor performs a Check upon a Reactor. We decompose each Check into two parts, an Action made by the Actor, and an opposing Reaction, made by the Reactor.

Every check in the game consists of an opposed action and reaction. When a PC attacks, checks to attack a monster, the character performs an action to attack and the monster performs a reaction to defend themselves. On the monsters turn, the monster might attack and the PC then performs a reaction to defend.

Ultimately the Action and the Reaction are resolved to numerical skill values and the higher of the two skill value prevails. In the interests of speed and simplicity of play when determining the skill values, usually, but not always, PCs will roll dice to determine their skill value, and antagonists will use a flat value, without rolling any dice.

playexample.p: When Dourli attacks a goblin with his axe then, Dourli is the Actor and the goblin is the Reactor. Dourli might attempt to perform this action with an Axe Cleave check and the Goblin might perform a Dodge Save, a reaction, to avoid being hit.

Subsequently, the goblin may try and stab Dourli with his short sword. Now the goblin is the Actor, Dourli is the Reactor, and the goblin might use a Sword Strike action while Dourli counters with a Shield Block Save.

indexentry.indexdefn: Players make Checks by rolling the dice to determine the outcome of actions in the game.
An Actor-Action-Reactor triplet is a structure for describing events, where an Actor (entity) attempts to perform an Action (verb) on an Reactor (target).
A Reactor is the object upon which an Actor performs an Action. When a PC strikes at a goblin with their sword, the goblin is the reactor of this action.
Anything that acts upon or may be acted upon in the game, PCs and antagonists, including environmental hazards etc.
An action is the verb being performed by the Actor upon the Reactor in a Check. The success or failure of an action is determined by comparing the results of the Check and the Save.

An actor, in the game, is any entity which may act upon another. During combat the Actor is usually the character whose turn it is. When a PC makes a Sword Strike against a goblin, then PC is the actor.

section.p: Making checks involves the following steps outlined below. We discuss these steps in detail in coming sections:

description.p: The actor decides what action they want to attempt, and selects a Check to perform that action.

Before a check can be made, the character must satisfy any prerequisites of that check, including having enough time (Action Points AP) to perform the action remaining in their turn, and having an appropriate rank in the ability to attempts the check.

descriptions.term: ii) The Reactor chooses a Save

description.p: After the actor decides what check they are using, the reactor(s) decide which Save they will use to oppose that check.
The reactor must be able to satisfy any prerequisites required by the Save including training and time requirements.
The check result is determined by comparing two skill results, the Actor's and the Reactor's.
Typically, Players involved in the check roll two different colored d20s. The darker die is the Fate die. The lighter die is the Skill die.
Antagonists, usually use a Flat DC for checks and counterchecks. Though they can roll a single D20 if the GM chooses.

descriptions.term: iv) Apply any Fate Die effects

description.p: High and low values on the fate die add special tags to the result including Blessed, Righteous, Damned and Cursed, which may be used to trigger other actions and effects. Similarly doubles add the Stars Align tag.
Certain Checks and Saves have a Point Pool cost, which may be affected by the Fate Die, and must be paid now.

The face value on the skill die is modified by the ability's rank, and any modifiers caused by fate, and point pool exhaustion. The results are made public so that players can choose whether they want to interrupt or respond to the result.

descriptions.description: Any triggered interrupts may be performed now, potentially modifying the skill values before the check results are finalized.
descriptions.term: vi) Resolve Check Results Apply Effects

description.p: The skill of the actor is compared with the skill of the reactor. The higher skill value succeeds. Any effects of the check are applied based on the check's level of success.

descriptions.description: Any triggered responses may be performed now.

subsection.p: Some antagonist abilities happen at the start of the players turn, represented by the following symbol . Start of Turn actions happen before any of the PCs actions and have no cost to the antagonists. Typically they are used to model ongoing conditions.
Each round characters get one Out-of-Turn Action (OOTAs). Certain abilities will allow characters to spend their OOTA to perform various Saves, Interrupts or Responses.

An Interrupt is an effect that happens before its' triggering action is resolved. A Save is a reaction that occurs at the same time as the Check and opposes it. While, a Response is an effect that happens after the triggering action has been resolved.
Intterupts, saves and interrupts can be Free, which means they do not require the character to spend their OOTA to perform. They are denoted by the following "hollow" symbols: , , and .

Responses and interrupts can be Mandatory, which means they must be performed if their prerequisites are met. Mandatory actions are denoted by a trailing exclamation mark and come in free and unfree types, , and .

section.p: First the Actor decides what action thet want to do, and then they choose a check to perform that action. Some negotiation with the GM may be necessary to ensure that the check is both Viable and Appropriate to the task at hand.

subsection.p: The Actor needs to make a choice about what check they want to make to try and perform an action. Most of the time the choice of which check to use should be fairly straightforward, to jump a horse over a fence you would make a check using the Riding ability, you swim using the Swim ability.

However, in some cases there may be multiple potential checks to choose from, and some negotiation between the GM and the player might be necessary to choose the most appropriate check to perform for a given action, to choose which Recall Knowledge Lore check to use from multiple Lore abilities, or to ask about range or reach of weapons, cover and so on.

When the choice of Check is not clear use the following rules of thumb:
Use the check that is most specific to the task at hand. If there is one ability specifically for performing the task at hand, use that ability. For example, when climbing use the Climb ability.
When the GM deems that there are multiple potential checks that might be used then the player may choose whichever check they prefer, and the GM should apply shifts to make the task harder when less relevant or appropriate checks are used for the task at hand. For example when trying to recall information about a nobles lineage, one character might make a check using History, while another might use Lore/Heraldry and the GM should allow either check.

indexentry.indexdefn: Viable Checks are checks that a character is allowed to perform. A check is viable if it satisfies a number of prerequisites that include having the time required to perform the action, having the required training to perform that action, having points towards any Pool Cost for the check, and any other prerequisites required for the check, within reach for melee attacks.

Most abilities require training before you can perform any checks associated with that ability. Abilities with an Untrained Rank do not require training and anyone can attempt to perform checks using those abilities at the untrained rank provided all other prerequisites are met.

subsection.p:
A check is Viable if all its prerequisite are satisfied:
The Actor must have time to perform the action. They must pay the Action Point Cost to perform the action. Each character gets five action points each turn. If they perform an action requiring three action points, then they cannot perform another three action point check in the same turn, because they do not have enough action points remaining to do so
The Actor must have any required rank in the ability required to make the check. Though some abilities can be used untrained, any ability with an Untrained Rank may be used untrained, most checks require a rank of at least one in an ability in order to perform a check, certain Alchemy checks have require ranks greater than one that must be met before the check can be made.
If the Check has a point pool cost then that pool must not be empty, in order to cast a spell which has a magic pool cost the character's magic pool must be greater than zero.
The actor must satisfy any other prerequistes specifically for that check, :
wielding a sword to use Sword Strike,
reactor within reach for melee attacks,
reactor within range for ranged attacks,
and any other requirements or preconditions listed in the check description
subsection.subsubsection:
Required Time
In order to perform an action a character must have enough time available to do so.
Outside of combat the rules deal with time informally. So it is up to the GM to determine how long a check will take, which might be in minutes, hours, days months or years.
During combat time is broken into 6 second Rounds. Characters get one Turn each round, and each turn is broken down into 5 Action Points (APs). The character can spend these action points to perform actions. If a character does not have the APs to perform a check they may not even attempt to perform that check.
Similarly each character gets one Out of Turn Action (OOTA) each round, which they may spend to perform responses, interrupts, and certain saves. More on these later.
Action Points (APs)
Combat time is broken down into 10 second rounds. During each round every combatant gets one turn.

subsubsection.p: By default checks require that the character have training in order to perform any checks associated with the ability, the character must have ranks in the ability to use it.
Some abilities may be used without training. Abilities with an Untrained value or a minimum rank of 0 do not require training to perform checks.

section.p: Once the a has chosen a check, the reactor chooses a Viable Save to counter. For example, if the actor makes a physical-attack the reactor has to choose one from a number of different physical-defence saves, Armour, Dodge, Shield Block, or Parry.

A save is viable in the same sense as a check is, except that instead of having an AP cost, saves are usually either free or have a response cost, that is they require that the reactor spend their out-of-turn action for that turn.

During each round every combatant gets one Out Of Turn Action that they can spend once to perform a certain checks outside of their turn.
Responses are Out of Turn Actions used to make certain Counter Checks.
Are Out-of-Turn Actions that occur before any results of a check are applied.
Are Out-of-Turn Actions that occur after any results of a check are applied.

subsection.p:
A Viable Saves satisfies the following conditions:
The Reactor must have any required rank for the check.
The Reactor must have an unused OOTA if their save requires one.
If the save has a point pool cost then then that pool must not be empty.
The actor must satisfy any other prerequistes specifically for the save, :
wielding a sword to use Sword Parry,
and any other requirments listed in the check description

section.p: The success or failure of an action is determined by comparing the Skill of the Actor and the Reactor.

subsection.p: There are three ways to evaluate the Skill in a check:
subsection.subsubsection:
Dynamic Skill Values
Players roll two different coloured d20s. The face value of the dark die is the Fate Value. The skill value is the face value of the lighter die plus the ability rank and any check modifiers. This is the only method players use to calculate skill.
GMs rarely use Dynamic Skill Values, but when they do the process is the similar to that for players except that GMs only roll a skill die. GMs never roll the Fate Die, instead they borrow Fate from the players.
Players make Dynamic Checks
The Skill is the face value of the Skill die, plus the characters ability rank and any shifts that apply, Dourli makes an attack, he rolls a 13 adds 3 for his rank to get a Skill of 16.
Calculating a Dynamic Skill Value.
For example, suppose Dourli rolls a 12 on his Skill Die while attacking with his Axe Strike 3 ability. The attack has no modifiers, there are no shifts. Then the Skill for that attack is 12 + 3 = 15.
Dourli Strikes with his Axe.
Later, Dourli rolls a 15 on his Skill Die while attacking the same Goblin with his Dagger Strike 2 ability. Unfortunately that goblin has ducked behind a small wall and the GM decides that this cover gives the attack two shifts down. Then the Skill for that attack is 15 + 2 - 4 = 13 with the -4 coming from the cover.
Dourli Stabs a Goblin in Cover.
{% include "docs/sidebars/shifts.xml" %}

subsubsection.p: Hidden Skill Values are used when the GM wants to make the outcome of a check uncertain to the players. This method of calculating skill is only used by Antagonists and differs from a Dynamic Skill Values only in that the skill dice result is not disclosed to the players, and no Fate die is rolled.

subsection.subsubsection:
Static Skill Values {% include "docs/sidebars/static_skill_values.xml" %} {% include "docs/sidebars/borrowing_fate.xml" %}
When calculating Static Skill Value we do not bother to roll the skill die, instead we assume that the die rolled a 10 and calculate the skill value as per usual. So the Static Skill is 10 plus the Rank of the Ability being used plus any shifts/modifiers. The static skill is Malleus Deums version of a DC. This is the usual way to calculate skill for Antagonists.
Static Checks are used by the GM for antagonists in order to save time, and by the GM for players in Hidden and Secret checks. Players should use the Roll Dice method instead.
Static Checks do not generate a Fate result. If the GM is making the static check for an antagonist, the antagonist borrows fate from the player. If the Static Check is made by the GM on behalf of a character in a hidden or secret check then assume a Fate Result of 10.
A goblin makes a Sword Strike 4 attack on Dourli, with no shifts. This gives the goblin a static skill (SSV) of 14 for his attack.
Calculating a Static Skill Value for the Goblin.
Dourli rolls 3 for his Fate and a 15 for his Skill, a Damned 15, using a shield block. The 15 succeeds in beating the goblins SSV of 14 so Dourli takes no damage.
However, the goblin can borrow Dourli's fate result, inverting it, the damned result for Dourli, becomes a Lucky result for the goblin. If the goblin had an interrupt or response that triggers on a Lucky fate value then he could perform that action.

subsection.p: There are the four different types of checks

subsubsection.p: Standard Checks are the workhorse of the game. The player rolls two dice and the GM uses a Static Skill Value.

If the GM wants to make the checks a little bit more random he can make opposed checks. In an Opposed Check the player and the GM both make dynamic checks, the player rolling two dice, the GM rolling a public skill die and borrowing fate.

A Hidden Check is an Opposed Check where the GMs skill die result is not revealled to the players. Hidden Checks may be used when the GM wants the players to remain uncertain about whether they have succeeded.

playexample.p: Dourli attempts to decieve, Emrich, the head of the local thieves guild and the GM does not want Dourli to know whether he succeeded or not.
Dourli checks his Deception, and gets a Skill of 18. Emrich rolls a 15 on his Perception Save and adds his Perception rank of 4 for a total of 19.
Now Dourli may be left thinking that there is a good chance he has fooled Emrich. But little does he know that, in fact, Emrich has seen through his ruse.

subsubsection.p: Secret Checks are made when the GM does not want the players to even know that a check has been made. The proceeds with the GM making a Hidden Skill Check for the antagonist and uses a Static Skill Value for the PCs result. No Fate result is generated or used.
An example of this might be Passive Perception checks may be made to have characters notice something about their environment without them asking to make the check.

section.p: To resolve the Fate Outcome check the face value of the Fate Die:

olist.li: A Natural 20 is Blessed and Lucky. The player gains the Blessings of Mithras boon.
A Natural 1 is Cursed and Damned. The player suffers Ill Omens bane.

section.p: If the Fate Die and Skill Die have the same Face Value, Doubles, then the Stars Align which trigger further actions.
The various fate results can trigger OOTAs for you, your allies and the NPCs. In addition, the fate values affect the Pool Point cost of checks as follows:

subsubsection.p: When the player rolls a Natural 20 on their Fate die they perform the Blessings of Mithras the player may choose one of the following boons:

descriptions.description: Halve the pool cost of the check or reduce the cost to zero if the cost is one.
Shift the Skill result up twice.
If this action is performed during a characters turn in combat then this check is free and requires no action points. If this action is a combat OOTA then it is free.

subsubsection.p: When Ill Omens occur the player must apply the first of the effects, that is applicable to the check, in the following list:

descriptions.description: If the check has an associated pool then increase the Pool Cost by one. If the check does not have an associated pool then this effect does not apply.
If the player has remaining action points after paying for this check then those points are lost. If the character does not have any remaining APs after this action then this effect does not apply.
Shift the Skill Die result down twice.

indexentry.indexdefn: Rolling doubles on a check adds the Stars-Align tag to the result.

subsubsection.p: Doubles gain the Stars Align tag which may trigger Out-of-Turn Actions.

Point Pool Cost
Check Point Pool Cost
Check Cost
Cost
Some checks have a cost in points that the character must pay from one of their point pools in order to make a check, casting spells usually costs points from the Magic Pool. You can tell if an action has an associated Point Pool by checking whether it has a Pool Cost or if it uses one the Point Pool keywords, Magic Pool. Checks made with those abilities may deduct the cost from the point pool, see .
subsection.subsubsection:
Exhaustion
{% include "docs/tables/exhaustion_table.xml" %}
If the point pool would be reduced below zero, then instead:
The pool value becomes zero, and
Shift the skill die down twice, and
Roll on the exhaustion table for that pool.
If the pool cost for a check is zero then performing the action usually has a negligable effect on the associated point pool. However the cost can still be affected by Fate and perhaps other factors.

section.p: Any interupts that are triggered happen now. Interrupts are OOTAs that occur before the triggering action. Interrupts count as OOTAs towards the action economy and in order to perform one a character has to spend their unused OOTA for the turn.
If an interrupt occurs and after the interrupt occurs the preconditions for the initial check are no longer met then the initial check automatically fails.

section.p: Responses happen now in reverse initiative order.
This section contains some extra details about using checks.

subsection.p: The GM should usually only require players to check when: the outcome is uncertain and failure would make the game more interesting .

Many tasks are easy enough that they can be completed automatically. In this case no check is required. Harder variants of the task might require a check though. For example, opening a door might be considered an easy task that automatically succeeds, while opening a door quietly might require a check. Similarly breaking down a door might require a check to perform quickly but can be done automatically given enough time, and that one of the characters carries an axe.
A problem arises that players will at times want to repeat checks until they succeed. We outline some strategies to deal with his.

In the usual course of play each character can perform a check once - twice if a reroll is used. For example, Dourli might try opening a box quickly by picking locks. If Dourli fails he might check to open the box with his axe but he can't try picking the lock again.

subsubsection.p: If the character will definitely succeed after making repeated attempts at a check and there is no other cost then just allow them to succeed, a character who can pick locks tries to open a cheap locked box that they have brought back to their lodgings. In this case the GM should perhaps not require a check at all. We call this approach Taking Time and if the GM thinks it is reasonable they should allow characters to announce they are Taking Time to perform a task.

subsubsection.subsubsectiontitle: Failure is Success with a Cost
subsubsection.p: If the player fails, they still succeed at the action, but with a "but", Yes, you find the secret door, but the noise attracts a guard, or Yes, you find the secret door, but it takes you so much time that the person you are chasing has fled, or Yes, you open the locked box but you break the lock, or you break your pick.
Each attempt has a cost associated with it. That cost might be time, money or increasing danger ( roll for random encounters at different times).

subsection.p: The most common form of check are Individual Checks, where the character performing the action makes the check. However, sometimes checks have to be made by a group of characters. In Malleus Deum there are two ways of doing this: Everyone Checks and Delegate Checks.

subsubsection.p: Sometimes everyone in a group has to make a check. For example, if the party is attacked using poisonous gas everyone in the group has to save individually. When Everyone Checks, each group member makes a separate check independent of the rest of the group and each individual suffers any repercussions separately if they fail.

In a delegate check one player character is Delegated by the GM to make a check on behalf of the whole group. If that check fails then the whole group fails the check. The GM may choose the delegate at random or at their own discretion. Some examples of checks that may be delegated are Initiative, Stealth, Perception, Ambush and Surprise rolls. But more on these later.

subsection.p:
Sometimes the players will get a chance to Reroll a Check. There are a number of rules about rerolling:
No check can be rerolled more than once for any reason
When rerolling all dice used to determine the initial result must be rerolled.
If the player rerolls the check they must take the result from the second roll.
Assume that all checks are able to be rerolled unless the ability states otherwise. Luck based checks cannot be rerolled.

indexentry.indexdefn: When taking fractional values always round up.
When taking fractional values always round up.

subsection.p: Some rules require numeric values to be halved, quartered and so on. When rounding the rule is always round up, half of 7 is 4, and a quarter of 7 is 2.

Advantage Disadvantage Some checks allow players to make checks at Advantage or at Disadvantage. In these cases an additional skill die is rolled (only one Fate die is ever rolled). When making a check with Advantage the player chooses the higher face value on the two skill dice as the Initial Skill Value. When making a check with Disadvantage the player chooses the lowest face value on the two skill dice as the Initial Skill Value.

In Malleus Deum all rules are optional, but some rules are more optional than others. Rules denoted by the dagger symbol are optional and may or may not be used as the GM prefers, trading off complexity and complications for speed of game play.
